source: van Opheusden, Galbiati, Kuperwajs, Bnaya, Li, Ma (2021 preprint of Nature 2023) Revealing the impact of expertise on human planning with a two-player board game
finding: In 4-in-a-row (4x9 board, about 1.2e16 states), a best-first search model with value pruning, feature dropout and noise fits human moves. Fitted planning depth (length of the principal variation) rises with skill and practice. Depth is 4 to 6 plies in lab players.
numbers: Learning experiment N=30, 5 sessions: Elo slope 21+-4.6 (p<0.001), depth slope 0.255+-0.061 per session (p<0.001), feature drop rate -0.0119+-0.0028. Depth, drop rate and heuristic quality together explain 56.7% of strength variance. Mobile app, 1000 users with 100+ games: depth slope 0.0108+-0.0010 (p<0.001). Model predicts held-out moves 40.8+-1.4% (N=40), 2AFC 58.6+-1.0%. Eye tracking N=10: r=0.535, branches reach up to 7 moves.
limits: Preprint text, not the Nature version. Depth is inferred from a fitted model, not observed. Authors note the 4-6 depth contradicts lower depths in earlier studies (Snider). One game, one lab.
agent_relevance: Pruning plus best-first is a working model of strong human play, and skill goes with deeper but still bounded search. Supports S6 depth as a budget parameter, not a fixed number.

source: van Opheusden et al. (2021 preprint) time-pressure and model-variant results
finding: Time pressure test of the depth measure: more time gives deeper plans but no better play, because players also overlook features more often at the long limit. Model variants Fixed iterations, Fixed depth and Fixed branching (a fixed beam) were fitted as alternatives to the stochastic best-first stopping and pruning rule.
numbers: Time pressure N=30, limits 5/10/20 s: depth slope 0.042+-0.018 (p=0.019); strength change -2.0+-1.6 Elo (p=0.21); feature drop rate rises 0.0027+-0.0010 (p=0.009). Computer opponents in the study use the Fixed branching pruning rule.
limits: The exact likelihood gap between the main model and the fixed-beam variants is in supplement tables that were garbled in the text extraction; not quoted. The drop-rate explanation is the authors' reading.
agent_relevance: Extra thinking time did not help when attention to features lapsed. For the agent: extra depth only pays if the evaluator keeps reading all features (re-read the state at each expansion).

source: Callaway, van Opheusden, Gul, Das, Krueger, Griffiths, Lieder (2022; preprint Dec 2021) Rational use of cognitive resources in human planning
finding: Planning is modelled as a metalevel decision problem. The optimal policy is near best-first search with a stopping rule that depends mostly on the gap between the best and the next-best path and only partly on the absolute value of the best path. Cost per expansion is the only key parameter. People are close to this.
numbers: Exp1 N=95 (Mouselab-MDP, 3-step plans, 8 start branches): people lose 0.92 points vs the best policy at the same click count, and beat random clicking by 4.94 points. Optimal model expands a max-value path 74.6-100% of the time (random 51.7%); people 81.5% (CI 79.6-83.3). Stop rule betas: best value 0.82, best-vs-next 1.68 (optimal model 0.99 and 4.64, so people under-use the gap). Cross-validated fit: optimal beats breadth-first, depth-first, random, myopic (LL diff >3981) and best-first (>1250); 45 participants best fit by optimal, 41 by a best-first variant, 9 other.
limits: Deterministic environments, plan-then-act. Pruning and depth limits were included only as extra heuristic mechanisms; the optimal model needs no explicit prune or depth cap. Best-first fits 41 of 95 people almost as well, so the data cannot separate the two for many people. Online sample (Prolific).
agent_relevance: Gives the concrete rule asked in gap 1: expand the best-looking path, stop when the leading path is clearly ahead of the runner-up (relative gap), with the threshold set by the cost of an expansion.

source: Callaway et al. (2021 preprint) Experiments 2-4: strategy adapts to reward structure
finding: The best classical strategy depends on where variance sits in the tree. Breadth-first is near-optimal when large rewards come early, best-first when variance is constant, depth-first when it comes late. People switched accordingly. A forward-search bias (92.4% of clicks on a state whose parent was already revealed, vs 75.5% in the model) was not costly.
numbers: Exp2 N=298 (three variance conditions, four paths of five steps); Exp3 N=93; Exp4 N=291 (travel-agent route text task). The optimal model fit best in every condition; with all heuristic mechanisms the optimal model still won in all but two cases (constant variance in Exp2 and Exp3). Violations of forward search 7.2% of the time, more likely when worth more (beta=2.48, z=5.48).
limits: Small trees (4 paths x 5 steps). Heuristics given distributional stop rules in a side analysis came close. No LLM test.
agent_relevance: A fixed beam is one of several strategies, each winning in only one reward structure. Supports letting S6 choose breadth versus depth from a cheap look at where the information sits, not a fixed width.

source: Chen, Li, Cakir, Akcali, Lee, Mattar (2026) Extracting Search Trees from LLM Reasoning Traces Reveals Myopic Planning (arXiv 2605.06840v5)
finding: First direct human-versus-LLM planning-depth comparison, on the same four-in-a-row task used for human depth. Reasoning-model traces (14 open-trace models, 9696 traces, 1092 games) were turned into search trees by a GPT-5 judge. LLM trees are shallow, and wins are predicted by breadth of first-move candidates, not depth.
numbers: 27 models in a round robin, 1404 games. Mean maximum depth 1.78+-0.71 plies (range 1.00-3.48) vs 4-6 inferred for humans. Regression on win rate: depth beta=-0.015 (p=0.82), breadth beta=0.075 (p=0.0025). GPT-OSS-120B at high vs medium reasoning effort: larger trees and higher win rate with identical weights.
limits: Trees come from an LLM judge reading the trace; validated on a human-annotated set but accuracy figures were not located in the text. One game; proprietary models excluded because traces are summaries. Preprint.
agent_relevance: For S6: LLM search effort that helps is more candidates, not more depth. A budget rule should buy breadth first.

source: Chen et al. (2026) cognitive-model fit and trace-pruning intervention
finding: A myopic model (score only the depth-1 states) predicts LLM moves better than full minimax over the extracted tree, for every model; the discount parameter goes to about zero. Deleting deep paragraphs of the chain of thought leaves the move unchanged; deleting the chosen branch changes it.
numbers: Myopic uniquely correct on 1236 turns vs 512 for full-tree. Intervention: remove final-decision paragraphs 2.1% move change; remove whole chosen branch 32.0%; remove largest unchosen branch 1.2%; add back depth-1 paragraphs only 4.1%; add deeper paragraphs too 3.7% (control 1.7%).
limits: One game, a judge-labelled intervention (Claude Opus 4.7 labels paragraphs), preprint. The human result it contrasts with is from d01 (model-inferred, not observed).
agent_relevance: Written-out deep lookahead may be decoration. A scaffold should force a backed-up value from the deeper node into the choice and test whether it changes the pick.

source: Wu, Sun, Yu, Welleck, Yang (2024/ICLR 2025) Inference Scaling Laws: compute-optimal inference for problem-solving with language models (arXiv 2408.00724)
finding: At matched inference FLOPs, MCTS with rollouts is worse than plain sampling with weighted voting. A reward-guided tree search without rollouts (REBASE: allocate children by softmax of step reward, prune low ones) beats sampling at every budget and reaches sampling accuracy with about 7x less compute for 7B models. Gains are small on easy problems and larger on hard.
numbers: MATH500 Table 1: Mistral-7B sampling 256 samples 8.70e14 FLOPs 42.8% vs REBASE 32 samples 1.36e14 FLOPs 45.0%; Llemma-7B 10.0e14 45.5% vs 1.48e14 46.8%; Llemma-34B 12.1e14 46.7% (64 samples) vs 7.08e14 49.2%. MATH-easy (levels 1-2): sampling and REBASE comparable; levels 3-5: REBASE clearly lower error (read from figure). MCTS needs 'dozens of times more generated tokens'.
limits: A trained process reward model supplies the step value, so this is verifier-plus-search, not a pure scaffold. Math only. The hard-versus-easy claim is read from Figure 8, with no table numbers.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 2: compared by FLOPs, not nodes, the part of search that wins is cheap step-level pruning with a value signal; deep rollouts lose. S6 should prune on a value, not roll out.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters (arXiv 2408.03314)
finding: Search against a process verifier: beam search beats best-of-N at small budgets, then the gap shrinks and reverses. On easy questions (bins 1-2) beam search gets worse with more budget (over-optimising the verifier); on medium and hard (bins 3-4) it beats best-of-N; on the hardest (bin 5) nothing helps. Lookahead (rollouts) underperforms at equal samples. Picking the method per difficulty bin nearly matches best-of-N with up to 4x less compute (16 vs 64 generations).
numbers: MATH, PaLM 2-S* base, PRM verifier. Budgets 4, 16, 64, 256 generations. Oracle and model-predicted difficulty bins gave overlapping curves. Search failure modes shown: low-information repeated steps and overly short 1-2 step solutions.
limits: Single base model family and a trained PRM; difficulty is estimated with the verifier from 2048 samples per question, which itself costs compute (acknowledged).
agent_relevance: Direct support for a difficulty gate on S6 (gap 10): open the tree for medium problems and low budgets, skip it for easy ones, and do not over-optimise a weak judge.

source: Feng, Wan, Wen, McAleer, Wen, Zhang, Wang (2023/ICML 2024) AlphaZero-like Tree-Search can Guide LLM Decoding and Training (TS-LLM, arXiv 2309.17179)
finding: A learned value function guides tree search better than prompting an LLM to score states. At equal tokens, the advantage over self-consistency with the same reward model shrinks on shallow tasks but stays on deeper ones.
numbers: Table 2 (BFS path@1): GSM8K LLaMA-SFT policy with LLaMA-V value 52.5% vs GPT-3.5 prompt value 45.8% vs LLaMA ToT value 37.4%; Game24 64.8% vs 21.0% vs 9.2%. Table 3 equal-token: Game24 CoT-SC with ORM 50.6% at 684 tokens vs MCTS-ORM 69.34% at 649 tokens; BFS-V-ORM 70.9% at 1.6k; PrOntoQA CoT-SC-ORM 83.2% at 273 vs MCTS-ORM 99.6% at 182. Authors: advantage 'largely decreases' vs CoT-SC-ORM, especially on GSM8K.
limits: Table text was garbled in extraction; values are matched by row order and should be rechecked against the PDF before quoting. LLaMA2-7B SFT and learned value networks, i.e. trained components. Chess endgame and RLHF tasks need deep search and show the largest gain.
agent_relevance: At equal tokens a searcher with a good state value beats best-of-k by a wide margin on Game of 24 and PrOntoQA and by little on GSM8K. Both parts matter: the value (checking) and the tree. Partial answer to gaps 2 and 9.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the Self-Verification Limitations of LLMs on Reasoning and Planning Tasks (arXiv 2402.08115)
finding: GPT-4 as its own verifier makes many wrong calls, and self-critique loops lower accuracy. A sound external verifier gives big gains and merely re-prompting with a sound verifier keeps most of the benefit.
numbers: 100 instances per domain. Game of 24 standard prompting 5%, LLM+LLM critique 3%, LLM+sound verifier 36-38%. Verifier accuracy on Game of 24 87.0% (3567/4100), false positives 10.4% (320/3071), false negatives 20.7% (213/1029); Blocksworld 72.4%, FPR 6.5%, FNR 15.48% (24/155); Mystery Blocksworld 71.8%, FPR 18.55%, FNR 97.09% (100/103). With chain-of-thought verification Game of 24 verifier accuracy 98.8%.
limits: GPT-4 (2023); Table 1 and 2 row labels partly garbled in extraction, so the domain pairing for the 95.8% FNR (probably graph colouring) is not certain. CoT verification changes the numbers a lot, so rates depend on the verify prompt.
agent_relevance: A judge that wrongly rejects 15-20% of true states (and 97% in a disguised domain) would remove the true path often. Gap 4: gives per-state false-negative rates, not per-path loss rates. Use code-checkable tests wherever possible.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning (arXiv 2412.06559)
finding: 3,400 expert-annotated solutions test whether a model can find the first wrong step. Open process reward models fall apart on harder sets; prompted critic LLMs are better; scores fall as problems get harder for every model.
numbers: F1 (GSM8K / MATH / OlympiadBench): Math-Shepherd-PRM-7B 47.9 / 29.5 / 24.8; Skywork-PRM-7B 70.8 / 53.6 / 22.9; Qwen2.5-Math-7B-PRM800K 68.2 / 62.6 / 50.7; GPT-4o-0806 79.2 / 63.6 / 51.4; o1-mini 93.2 / 88.9 / 87.2. GPT-4o average 61.9. Many correct final answers still hide a wrong step, more often on harder sets.
limits: Table 3 column order was recovered from a garbled layout; the Omni-MATH column and averages for most rows are not quoted. Math only. Measures first-error finding, not how often a prune-by-score rule drops the true path.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partial: a step judge is weakest exactly on the hard problems where trees are wanted. Pruning with a small judge on hard items will cut true paths often; a revisit list or a larger judge is needed.

source: Ma et al. (2026) CoT2-Meta: Budgeted Metacognitive Control for Test-Time Reasoning (arXiv 2603.28135)
finding: A training-free controller with expand, prune, repair and stop decisions over a thought tree. Ablation at a fixed call cap: removing pruning lowers accuracy and raises tokens. Token-matched control: extra search expansion with the same tokens does not match selective repair.
numbers: Cap C=16 calls. Full 92.8 MATH / 90.4 GPQA / 75.8 BBEH at 5,280 tokens; single chain (no tree) 78.5 / 74.2 / 65.4 at 1,929 tokens; no process evaluator 86.5 / 82.3 / 69.3 at 9,850 tokens; no metacognitive pruning 88.2 / 84.1 / 71.3 at 6,430 tokens (row-to-token alignment in the garbled table is uncertain). Table 20 MATH N=500: no repair 73.4% at 4,650 tokens, no repair plus extra expansion (matched) 74.6% at 5,290, full selective repair 77.1% at 5,280.
limits: Single preprint with very high headline numbers. The prune precision and false-prune audit are shown only as a figure; no numbers in the text. The single-chain arm uses 1 call vs about 15 for the tree, so it is not a matched-token arm.
agent_relevance: The cleanest matched-token ablation found: pruning is worth a few points and some thousand tokens inside the same system, and extra unfocused expansion gains only 1.2 points. Unverified by others. Gaps 2 and 4 partial.

source: Kim, Huang, Reza, Grand (2025) Chopping Trees: Semantic Similarity Based Dynamic Pruning for Tree-of-Thought Reasoning (SSDP, arXiv 2511.08595) - full re-read of tables and limits
finding: Merging near-duplicate sibling steps (embedding similarity, one hand-set threshold) cuts nodes and time on small open models in maths. The authors themselves list the limits that gap 7 asks about.
numbers: Qwen2.5-1.5B average nodes per sample: MATH500 DPTS generated 214.4, explored 53.3; SSDP 31.1 and 11.5. GSM8K DPTS 79.1 / 19.5; SSDP 9.4 / 4.8. So generated nodes fall about 85% and explored nodes about 78% on MATH500. Time ratio vs their baseline: Llama family 5.87x, Qwen 4.77x. Table 1 SSDP accuracy is within about 5 points of the best method; the SSDP row values in the extraction are garbled.
limits: Models: Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-1.5B and 7B only. Math only (GSM8K, MATH500). Authors write: similarity does not imply equivalence, threshold is dataset- and model-dependent, over-pruning is not fully quantified, other domains and families remain an open question. No closed model tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open: no evidence for large closed models or non-math tasks. Corrects the first-pass 85-90% fewer nodes: true for generated nodes on MATH500, about 78% for explored.

source: Setlur, Nagpal, Fisch, Geng, Eisenstein, Agarwal, Agarwal, Berant, Kumar (2024) Rewarding Progress: Scaling Automated Process Verifiers for LLM Reasoning (arXiv 2410.08146)
finding: A step score defined as progress (change in the chance of finishing correctly before and after the step, measured under a separate prover policy) searches better than an outcome reward. Weak provers can still help a stronger base model.
numbers: Process advantage verifiers vs outcome reward models: about 5x more compute-efficient and 8-10% more accurate in test-time beam search; 6x more sample-efficient and 7% better in online RL. Earlier automated PRMs gain only 1-2% over ORMs.
limits: Trained verifiers on Gemma-family policies, MATH. Not a prompt-only scheme. The abstract says 10% and the body says 8%; not reconciled here.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a relative-progress score is a better signal for choosing which branch to widen than an absolute score, which matches BAVT. The LLM-only proxy (ask the model what progress this step made) is not tested here.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking: Understanding the Strengths and Limitations of Reasoning Models via the Lens of Problem Complexity (arXiv 2506.06941)
finding: On Tower of Hanoi, Checker Jumping, River Crossing and Blocks World, accuracy falls to zero beyond a model-specific size for both thinking and non-thinking models, even when the algorithm is given in the prompt. Three regimes: simple (non-thinking as good or better and cheaper), medium (thinking helps), hard (both collapse).
numbers: Collapse near Hanoi N=8 (255 moves); River Crossing fails at N=3 (11 moves) while Hanoi N=5 (31 moves) is near perfect; thinking tokens fall near the collapse point; 64k token cap. Giving the solution algorithm did not move the collapse point (Fig 8).
limits: Contested, see d16. River Crossing instances for N>=6 are unsolvable (Lawsen). Answer format (full move lists) confounds depth with output length. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 partial: a depth at which unaided LLM internal search collapses exists on these puzzles, but its cause is disputed. Do not set an S6 depth cap from this alone.

source: Lawsen (2025) The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking: a comment on Shojaee et al. (arXiv 2506.09250)
finding: Argues the collapse is mostly an experiment artefact: output token limits for exhaustive move lists, an automatic grader that cannot tell stopped from cannot, and unsolvable River Crossing instances (N>=6 with boat capacity 3). Asking for a program that prints the Hanoi solution gave high accuracy at N=15.
numbers: Hanoi about 10 tokens per move, so a 64k cap allows N=12-13 if only the final move list is printed. Preliminary test, N=15 Hanoi as a Lua function: very high accuracy for Claude 3.7, Claude Opus 4, o3, Gemini 2.5 in under 5,000 tokens (no per-model numbers given).
limits: Short comment; no systematic numbers or sample sizes; the author says an earlier version had token-arithmetic errors and was partly written by an AI model. Weak as evidence on its own, strong on the River Crossing arithmetic.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: planning depth in LLMs is confounded with answer format. A compact plan form (procedure or function) pushes the usable depth much further than listing every step. Supports sub-plan caching as an idea, with no cached-result test.

source: Lavalley, Mehta, Taylor, Chuning, Stewart, Huys, Khalsa, Paulus, Smith (2025) Computational mechanisms underlying multi-step planning deficits in methamphetamine use disorder (Transl Psychiatry)
finding: New site (Laureate Institute, Tulsa) and new sample use the Huys planning task and fit the same pruning parameter. People with methamphetamine use disorder prune more after large losses than healthy controls, and craving after an anxiogenic breathing-resistance task predicts more pruning.
numbers: 40 patients vs 49 healthy participants, two runs each (with and without breathing resistance). Group effect on aversive pruning eta_p^2=0.14, post-hoc Cohen's d=0.81; Group x Resistance F(1,90)=5.17, p=0.025, eta_p^2=0.05 (patients pruned more without resistance).
limits: Same task and modelling approach; Huys is a co-author, so not lab-independent. It tests a group difference, not whether healthy people prune. Different site and sample, which is a real replication of the parameter's relevance.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: closest to an outside replication, but still the same paradigm. No different-task test.

source: Zorowitz, Momennejad, Daw (2020) Anxiety, avoidance, and sequential evaluation (Computational Psychiatry 4:1-17)
finding: An independent group (Daw lab) shows by simulation that an agent with a pessimistic belief about its own later choices reproduces Huys-style pruning of the better branch without any pruning mechanism or failure to look. Anxiety, not depression, is the link they model.
numbers: Model prediction of Fig 3b: increasing pessimism makes the agent give up large later gains after an early loss. Authors state that the link of pruning to depressive or anxiety symptoms differs depending on the study.
limits: Theory and simulation only; no new human data. Authors suggest slight variants of the decision trees could tell the two accounts apart, but that was not run.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: no independent empirical test, but an independent, testable rival account: the loss branch is undervalued because the agent expects to choose badly later. A scaffold can guard against this by asking what it would do after that step before cutting.

source: Brown, Juravsky, Ehrlich, Clark, Le, Re, Mirhoseini (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling (arXiv 2407.21787)
finding: With an automatic verifier, simply sampling more answers raises the fraction solved a lot. Without one, majority voting and reward models stop gaining after about 100 to a few hundred samples.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with one sample to 56% with 250 samples (single-sample state of the art 43%). Coverage grows log-linearly in samples. One math task: 98.44% coverage with 10,000 samples.
limits: Coverage is not accuracy; without a checker the gain is not captured. Repeated sampling only, no tree.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: much of the gain is the check, not the search. Where a code or rule check exists, the plain-sampling baseline is strong and search must beat it at equal tokens.

source: Search log for gaps 3 and 9: no paper found
finding: Queries on arXiv and Europe PMC (loss aversion, Pavlovian, Huys, bonsai, resource-rational, depth and humans with language models; leaf value and cut-branch value in LLM trees) returned no study that runs the Huys loss-driven pruning task on an LLM, and none that tests a one-line guess or cached value for a cut branch against a zero value at equal tokens. The only human-versus-LLM depth comparison found is d05-d06. WebSearch was out of budget; OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited, so coverage is by arXiv and Europe PMC queries only.
numbers: Zero hits for the two target topics across about 20 queries; hits came only for neighbours (d05, d13, d12).
limits: An absence claim from a limited tool set. A missed 2026 paper is possible. Not the same as no such work exists.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 9 stay open. Treat an affective-pruning guard and a cut-branch leaf value as designed-in tests to run on the agent, not as rules with outside evidence.
